title: A Wall That Listens
sum: Atrahasis brings a dream to his god Enki and asks what it means. Enki is bound by the gods' oath not to tell any human that a flood is coming, so he speaks to the reed wall of Atrahasis' house instead: leave the house, build a boat, reject possessions and keep life alive. He sets a water clock running and tells of the seven nights of the flood.

Atrahasis calls the elders of his town and gives them a cover story: his god and theirs have quarreled, so he must leave Enlil's land and go down to the Apsu with Enki. The whole town helps build the boat. He loads silver and gold, clean animals, birds and wild creatures, holds a feast for his people, and puts his family aboard. While the guests eat and drink he cannot sit still for grief. Adad thunders, Atrahasis seals the door with pitch, and the wind snaps the mooring rope.
readings: The outline is the same as Noah's: a warning from heaven, a vessel built to a god's plan, animals and family aboard, a door sealed, and the storm. Almost every detail is turned, though. Genesis has one God who both judges and warns, and gives a reason, the violence that filled the earth (Genesis 6:11-13). Here one god warns behind the backs of the others, through a wall, and the hero hides the truth from his neighbors.
Read as a story about secrecy

Everything in this chapter is half-hidden: a dream, a speech to a wall, a riddling promise of "rain," an excuse to the elders, a feast whose guests do not know it is a farewell. The poet seems to enjoy the cleverness. The cost is that the townspeople, who build the boat with their own hands, are left to die.

views.C: A Christian reader sees a true memory bent out of shape. In Genesis the God who sends the flood is the God who warns, so justice and mercy are not split between rival gods; Noah is warned openly, builds in faith, and becomes "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5), and through the building "he passed sentence on the world" (Hebrews 11:7). Atrahasis is warned in secret and keeps the secret. The Bible's God gives the world time and warning; he "wants everyone to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4).
views.H: Assyriologists note that this column is preserved in two pieces of Ipiq-Aya's tablet (C1 and C2) and can be compared with the Ark Tablet, the Middle Babylonian copies from Ugarit, Hattusa and Nippur, and Gilgamesh XI, which follows the same speech closely: wall, house, boat, possessions, life (Gilgamesh XI 20-31, Heidel). Alexander Heidel wrote in 1949 that "the most widely accepted explanation today" was that the biblical account is based on Babylonian material (Heidel, p. 261), though he himself judged the evidence to prove no more than a "genetic relationship" (p. 268). A. R. Millard, in his 1966 Tyndale lecture, argued instead that borrowing "has yet to be shown" and that both remember one real flood, with Genesis the more probable account.
views.M: For the first hearers Enki was the shrewd god of the fresh waters and of craft, the patron who looks after humans, and the hero's personal god. A dream was a normal way for a god to speak; the water clock, the elders at the gate, the reed house and the boat coated with bitumen all belonged to their world. The gods' oath was binding, so Enki's trick of speaking to a wall would have been admired as clever, not condemned as a lie.
views.S: Some Christian readers hold that the gods of the nations were real spiritual powers (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20): Justin Martyr wrote that people who did not know the evil demons for what they were "called them gods" (First Apology 5). Read that way, Enki is a power that imitates God's role as warner while working against the high god of its own pantheon. Read with Psalm 96:5, "Every god of the peoples is a nothing-god," the story is human memory and imagination, not a report from the unseen world. Both readings agree that the true warning came from the one God (Genesis 6:13).
views.J: Jewish writers told the warning very differently. 1 Enoch has the Most High send Uriel to Noah to say "Hide yourself" and to teach him how to escape (1 Enoch 10:1-3), and in the Animal Vision a heavenly being "taught him a secret" before he built his boat (1 Enoch 89:1). The rabbis say Noah built openly for 120 years and warned his neighbors (Genesis Rabbah 30:7; Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 108b). Berossus, a Babylonian priest writing in Greek, keeps the dream and the cover story: if asked, the hero should say he is sailing to the gods to pray for men.

deep.h: The boat in the different versions
deep.b:
Ipiq-Aya's copy keeps only a few words of the plan: "equal" and "a circle" (10:19, 10:21), a roof "like the Apsu," strong fittings and thick pitch. The Ark Tablet gives the whole plan: a circle, length and breadth equal, a floor of one ikû and walls one nindanu high, with ribs, cabins and huge amounts of bitumen, a giant coracle. The Nippur copy says to build it of good reed and calls it "Preserver of Life." Gilgamesh XI makes it a cube with six decks and seven stories. Genesis 6:15 gives a long box, 300 by 50 by 30 cubits.

The Mesopotamian vessels match the river craft of Iraq, round reed boats and barges. Genesis' proportions are those of a ship meant to ride out a sea. Readers who take Genesis as history see in that a mark of a sober record; critical readers see in it the priestly writer's love of measured order.

The New Testament stresses that Noah was warned and acted in faith (Hebrews 11:7), that God waited patiently "while the ark was being made ready" (1 Peter 3:20), and that Noah was "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5). Atrahasis' god has to hide his warning; Atrahasis has to hide it again from his neighbors (10:35-43), and the neighbors build the boat and come to his feast without knowing. The difference is not just in the plot but in the gods: Enki can only save by stealth; the LORD saves openly, in his own name.

deep.title: The feast and the shut door (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is Claude's reading. Jesus' words about the days of Noah (Matthew 24:37-39; Luke 17:26-27) have two details that Genesis does not: people eating and drinking up to the day Noah went in, and the suddenness of the shut door. Both are vivid in this chapter: the feast where "The eater ate; / the drinker drank" (10:70-71) and the door sealed as the storm breaks (10:78-79). This does not mean that Jesus knew Atrahasis. More likely, eating and drinking at a feast is simply how any story would show ordinary life going on before a disaster, and the Gospels use it independently. The overlap is worth noticing, not building on.

echoes: Genesis 6:13-22; Genesis 7:1-16; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:20; 2 Peter 2:5; Matthew 24:37-39; Luke 17:26-27; Exodus 2:3; Psalm 29:10; 1 Enoch 10:1-3; 1 Enoch 89:1

settings.what: Atrahasis asks the meaning of his dream
settings.when: after the gods have sworn to bring the flood (chapter 9)
settings.why: To learn what the dream means, "its head and its tail": the request gives Enki an opening to speak without breaking the oath.
settings.readers: The copy was written by Ipiq-Aya, a junior scribe at Sippar, in the twelfth year of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon (his colophon, 12:104-115; SEAL), in the 1600s BC (Millard). Its first readers were scribes in training and the temple and palace circles they served; later copies from Ugarit, Hattusa and Nippur show that the story travelled far in the next centuries.

settings.what: Enki's message to the reed wall
settings.to: the reed wall of Atrahasis' house, with Atrahasis listening
settings.when: at once, in answer to the dream
settings.why: To warn one man and give him the plan of the boat while keeping the letter of the gods' oath; the words are addressed to a wall so that Enki can later say he told no human.
settings.readers: For the scribes who copied the poem (see the card at 10:1-7), the speech to the wall showed Enki's cleverness in keeping the letter of a sworn oath.
views: A clever loophole that saves life.
A warning that has to be smuggled, set against the open warning God gives Noah (Genesis 6:13-21).

settings.to: the elders of his town, gathered at his gate
settings.when: after Enki's instruction, before the boat is built
settings.why: To explain why he is leaving and to get the town's help, without revealing the flood: his god and the town's god have quarreled, so he will go down to the Apsu with Enki. The town builds the boat for him (10:46-49).
settings.readers: Readers of the copy (see 10:1-7) see a man leave his city under his god's protection without giving away a sworn secret.

title: Seven Days and Seven Nights
sum: The flood breaks. Something with talons rips the sky, the land's noise is smashed like a pot, and the destruction sweeps over the people like a battle. In the dark no one can see his brother; the drowned float like flies. The gods themselves are terrified by the noise of the flood. They flee into the sky and huddle around Anu, who has lost his wits.

Nintu, also called Mami, the goddess who made humankind, weeps. She cannot believe she voted for total destruction in the assembly; Enlil pressed her into it. Where is Anu, she asks, who let his sons bring the flood without thinking? Her children fill the sea like dragonflies and drift like rafts against the banks. The other gods weep with her, hungry and thirsty, for no one is left to feed them. For seven days and seven nights the storm rages. Then the tablet breaks off.
readings: Genesis tells the flood like a log: dates, depths, days (Genesis 7:11-24). Atrahasis tells it as a lament, from heaven's side, with frightened, hungry gods. Genesis never shows God afraid or hungry; it shows him remembering Noah and sending a wind (Genesis 8:1).
Read as the poem's own judgment

The poet lets the mother goddess condemn the flood: it was rash, unthinking, a betrayal of her children. A. R. Millard notes that after the flood the gods, "already regretting their action," fell to blaming one another. The gods regret their decision because it was wrong; in Genesis God is grieved by human evil before the flood (Genesis 6:6) and does not call the judgment a mistake.

views.C: Here the Christian reader feels the distance most. These gods are overwhelmed by their own act, sit hungry because their servants are dead, and blame one another. The Bible's God is never at the mercy of the waters: "At the Flood the LORD took his throne" (Psalm 29:10), and he does not need offerings: "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you" (Psalm 50:12). Yet the poem's grief is real and humane. Nintu's tears for her children are a faint echo of a truer grief, the LORD's pain at human evil (Genesis 6:6) and Jesus' tears over his city (Luke 19:41).
views.H: This column is preserved only on C1. Gilgamesh XI tells the same storm in closely matching words: the land broken like a pot, the battle, no one seeing his fellow, the gods cowering, the mother goddess's lament and "the spawn of fish" filling the sea (Heidel). The storm lasts seven days and nights here and in the Sumerian Flood Story, against forty days of rain in Genesis 7:12. Heidel judged that the Babylonian stories show gods "prompted more by caprice than by a sense of justice" (Heidel, p. 268); the poem's own goddess seems to agree.
views.M: For Babylonians the gods lived on the offerings brought to their temples each day: bread, meat, beer, incense. A world without humans was a world without temple meals, and the poem draws that out without embarrassment. The mother goddess, invoked by women in childbirth, grieves as a mother would. Her title "midwife of the gods" and the picture of the gods huddled like sheep at a trough show a religion that pictured its gods in human terms.
views.S: Christian readers who see the nations' gods as fallen powers (Michael Heiser reads Deuteronomy 32:8, with the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint, as setting the nations under divine beings, "sons of God," who are judged in Psalm 82; Justin Martyr wrote that people who did not know the evil demons for what they were "called them gods" (First Apology 5)) may read the panic in heaven as the poet's sense that these powers do not control the world they claim. Paul says Christ "stripped the rulers and the authorities bare" (Colossians 2:15), and Psalm 82 pictures the gods of the nations judged and dying like men. Read with Psalm 96:5, the scene is only a human picture of heaven drawn from a royal court in crisis.
views.J: Jewish tradition kept the darkness and terror of the flood but put God in command of it. The Talmud says the waters of the flood were hot, and that the seven days before it were a mourning for Methuselah (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 108b). 1 Enoch makes the flood God's cleansing of a world corrupted by the Watchers (1 Enoch 10:2; 106:15-17). None of these writings show God hungry or afraid.

deep.b:
Atrahasis is built on one idea: humans were made to do the gods' work and feed them (chapter 3). The flood therefore starves the gods. Nintu thirsts for beer; the Anunnaki sit "thirsty and starving" and crowd like sheep at a trough (11:29, 11:67-73). When the offering comes, they gather like flies (12:8).

The Bible answers this picture head-on. "Do I feed on the flesh of strong bulls? / Do I drink goats' blood?" (Psalm 50:13). Moses mocks the gods "who ate the fat of their sacrifices" (Deuteronomy 32:38). Paul tells the Athenians that God is not served by human hands "as if he were short of anything" (Acts 17:25). In Genesis 8:21 God smells Noah's offering, but he is not fed by it; he answers with a promise to the whole earth.

deep.h: A mother who grieves, a Father who saves
deep.b: Nintu is the most sympathetic god in the poem. She shaped humankind, she weeps for them, and she condemns the flood. But she also voted for it (11:34-36), and her grief changes nothing for the drowned. The Bible gives a different picture of God's heart. He grieves before judgment, over evil (Genesis 6:6); he spares a family and a remnant of every kind; he promises never to flood the earth again (Genesis 9:11); and the prophets compare his compassion to a mother's that cannot forget (Isaiah 49:15). In the New Testament the grief and the rescue meet in one person, who weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41) and gives his life for the world (John 3:16).

echoes: Genesis 7:11-24; Genesis 8:1; Genesis 6:6; Exodus 10:23; Psalm 29:10; Psalm 50:12-13; Amos 5:18-20; Isaiah 54:9; Acts 17:24-25; Luke 19:41

settings.by: Nintu, called Mami, the mother goddess
settings.to: herself and the gods huddled in the sky; aimed at Anu and Enlil
settings.when: during the storm, as the gods hide in the sky
settings.why: To mourn the humans she made and to put the blame where she thinks it belongs: on herself for voting for the flood, on Enlil for pressing her, on Anu for letting his sons act without thinking.
settings.readers: The copy was written by Ipiq-Aya, a junior scribe at Sippar, in the twelfth year of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon (his colophon, 12:104-115; SEAL), in the 1600s BC (Millard). Its first readers were scribes in training and the temple and palace circles they served; later copies from Ugarit, Hattusa and Nippur show that the story travelled far in the next centuries.
views: Many readers take the lament as the poet's verdict that the flood was a rash act of the gods.
An honest cry against cruelty, set against the Bible's God, whose judgments are "true and just" (Revelation 16:7).

settings.to: the gods, over the drowned land
settings.why: To grieve over her children floating like dragonflies and rafts, and to wish another had borne them.
settings.readers: For the poem's readers (see the card at 10:1-7), the pictures of dragonflies and rafts belong to the river country where the copy was made.

title: Flies Over the Offering
sum: After a long break the flood is over. Atrahasis makes an offering to the four winds. The starving gods smell it and crowd like flies over the offering. When they have eaten, Nintu rises to rebuke them all, Enlil most of all: he did not think, he brought the flood. She takes up the big flies that Anu once hung on her necklace and makes them the lapis lazuli of her neck, so that she will remember these days.

Enlil sees the boat and explodes: the gods were under oath; how did a man live? Anu names Enki. Enki admits it proudly and turns the charge around: Enlil acted without thinking; punish the guilty, not everyone. Enlil gives way and asks Enki and Nintu to settle the future in the assembly. Enki decrees a new order: some women will not bear, the demon Pashittu will snatch babies, and orders of priestesses will be forbidden to have children. The poem ends as a song in praise of the god's counsel, "Listen!", and with Ipiq-Aya's note: 1,245 lines in three tablets.
readings: Many of the same elements come after the flood in both: an offering, the divine smelling of it, a decision about the future, and a sign in heaven tied to remembering. The order is not the same. Here the necklace comes before Enlil's anger and the new order; in Genesis God's promise and blessing come first and the bow last (Genesis 8:20-9:17). Much of this part of the poem is also broken (12:1, 12:53, 12:90). The content is turned the other way. The gods eat; God makes a promise. The goddess hangs up a necklace to remember her grief; God sets his bow in the clouds to remember his covenant. The gods limit human births; God blesses Noah: "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1).

The poem began with gods worn out by work and annoyed by noise. It ends with a lasting settlement: humans keep doing the work and feeding the gods, but their numbers are held down by barrenness, infant death and celibate priestesses, so that floods are no longer needed. The poem explains why life is as it is in its first hearers' world.

views.C: A Christian reads this chapter as the point where Atrahasis and Genesis part most clearly. In Atrahasis the gods solve the human problem by shrinking humanity; in Genesis God renews his blessing, binds himself by covenant to every living creature, and sets the bow in the clouds (Genesis 9:1-17). The human problem in Genesis is not numbers but the evil of the heart (Genesis 8:21), and God's answer, worked out through the rest of Scripture, is not fewer children but a new heart and a Savior (Ezekiel 36:26; Romans 5:12-21). The poem's gods eat the offering; the Bible's sacrifices point to the one offering Christ made "a soothing smell" to God (Ephesians 5:2).
views.H: Tikva Frymer-Kensky read the end of the poem as its point: the problem behind all the disasters was overpopulation, Enki's permanent measures are the poem's solution, and Genesis rejects it with its command to be fruitful. Millard, writing when less was known, saw the gods "already regretting their action" and noted that the Gilgamesh line "On the sinner lay his sin" did not occur in the Atrahasis text then known; this column now preserves the matching command (12:50). On how Genesis relates to this tradition, Heidel judged the evidence to prove nothing beyond a "genetic relationship" (Heidel, p. 268), and Millard that borrowing "has yet to be shown."
views.M: For the first hearers the new order explained things they saw every day: barren women, babies who died, and the respected orders of temple women, the entu, ugbabtu and others, who did not bear children. These were not seen as evils without reason but as part of a settlement made by the gods after the flood. The flies of lapis lazuli and the year name of the colophon, with the king's statues in a temple, show a world where gods were honored with costly images.
views.S: Christian readers who see real powers behind the gods (Justin Martyr wrote that people who did not know the evil demons for what they were "called them gods" (First Apology 5); Michael Heiser reads Deuteronomy 32:8, with the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint, as setting the nations under divine beings, "sons of God," who are judged in Psalm 82) may note that the poem's last decree is the creation of a demon to seize infants. The Bible never credits God with such a decree; it places the little ones under heavenly care (Matthew 18:10) and promises a world where "No more will there be in it / a baby who lives only a few days" (Isaiah 65:20). Read with Psalm 96:5, the demon is the poem's way of naming a sorrow, infant death, that it could not explain otherwise.
views.J: Berossus ends his flood story with the hero taken to live with the gods because of his reverence and a voice from the air telling the survivors to fear the gods. The rabbis taught that "the descendants of Noah," that is, all humanity, were given seven commandments, among them the ban on bloodshed (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 56a): a law for all nations, not a limit on births.

deep.h: After the flood: Atrahasis and Genesis 8-9 side by side
deep.b:
The offering. Atrahasis offers to the four winds (12:3-5); Noah builds an altar to the LORD and offers clean animals (Genesis 8:20).

The smell. "The gods smelled the scent" (12:7); "The LORD smelled the soothing smell" (Genesis 8:21).

The reaction. The gods crowd like flies and eat (12:8-9); Nintu rebukes them (12:10-18). The LORD speaks "in his heart" a promise not to curse the ground again (Genesis 8:21-22).

The sign. The goddess makes the lapis flies her necklace "so that I may remember" (12:19-29). In Genesis the sign comes last: God sets his bow in the clouds "and remember the covenant" (Genesis 9:12-17).

The new order. After Enlil's anger and Enki's defense (12:30-56), the gods limit births by barrenness, infant death and celibate priestesses (12:68-76). God blesses Noah's family to be fruitful and fill the earth, and protects human life by law (Genesis 9:1-7), before the bow.

So the two accounts share these elements, but not their order, and much of this part of the poem is broken (12:1, 12:53, 12:90). How they are related is debated. Heidel judged that the Babylonian and Hebrew versions are "genetically related" (p. 260), and noted that "the most widely accepted explanation" in his day was that the biblical account is based on Babylonian material (p. 261); he himself concluded that the evidence proves no more than the genetic relationship (p. 268). Millard held that "the two accounts undoubtedly describe the same Flood," that borrowing "has yet to be shown," and that Genesis keeps the more probable account. On the central questions, who sends the flood and who saves, whether the gods need food, and whether human numbers are the problem, Genesis gives the opposite answer.

deep.title: From a necklace of flies to a bow of promise (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is Claude's reading. The goddess's necklace and God's bow have more in common than a sign in heaven: both are ornaments or weapons of a god hung up after battle. The note on Genesis 9:13 reports that many scholars read the bow there as God's weapon, hung up and pointed away from the earth as a sign of peace. The Atrahasis poem ends with a speaker who "stirred up battle" (12:97). If Genesis answers this tradition, the answer is pointed: the Babylonian goddess hangs up the dead as jewels to feed her grief; the God of Israel hangs up his weapon as a pledge of peace for the living. The weapon reading of Genesis 9:13 is set out in the Genesis note; tying it to the necklace of Atrahasis is Claude's suggestion.

echoes: Genesis 8:20-22; Genesis 9:1-17; Leviticus 1:9; Psalm 50:12-13; Genesis 18:25; Ezekiel 18:20; Isaiah 54:9; Deuteronomy 23:17; Psalm 113:9; Ephesians 5:2

settings.what: Nintu's complaint and her vow by the necklace
settings.to: all the gods gathered at the offering, and Enlil in particular
settings.when: after the gods have eaten Atrahasis' offering
settings.why: To shame the gods, above all Enlil, for the flood, and to bind herself never to forget it, making the flies of her necklace a memorial.
settings.readers: For the poem's readers (see the card at 10:1-7), lapis lazuli was a costly stone fit for a goddess; the scene gives the flood a memorial kept in heaven.

settings.to: the gods, and the Igigi in particular
settings.why: To find out who broke the oath and how a man survived.
settings.readers: The readers (see 10:1-7) learn that even the chief god could be outwitted, and that the gods' sworn secret could get out.

settings.why: To point to the obvious culprit, the god who speaks through reed walls.
settings.readers: The scene names the god the readers (see 10:1-7) knew as the shrewd patron of wisdom and craft.

settings.to: the great gods, and Enlil directly
settings.why: To own what he did, to accuse Enlil of acting without thought, and to argue that punishment should fall on the guilty only.
settings.readers: The readers (see 10:1-7) hear from a god, to the chief of the gods, that punishment belongs to the guilty.
views: A clever god wins the argument for mercy.
A true principle, "the person who sins" bears the guilt (Ezekiel 18:20), spoken by a god who had sworn to the flood himself.

settings.why: To settle the matter by having Enki and the birth goddess plan a new order in the assembly.
settings.readers: The scene shows the readers (see 10:1-7) the gods settling matters by council, as they did when they decreed the flood (chapter 9).

settings.what: Enki's decree for the new order
settings.when: in the assembly after the flood
settings.why: To make a lasting limit on human numbers: barren women, a demon who takes infants, and priestesses forbidden to bear children. It explains to the first hearers sorrows and institutions they knew.
settings.readers: For the readers (see 10:1-7), the decree gave a reason for things in their own cities: barren women, infants who died, and orders of priestesses who did not bear children.
views: Frymer-Kensky: the measures solve the poem's real problem, too many people.
Others stress the gods' wish for quiet and order more than numbers.

settings.to: the counselor of the gods, probably Enki; the Igigi; and "all the people"
settings.when: at the end of the poem
settings.why: To praise the god whose counsel saved life and to present the whole poem as a song about the flood for everyone to hear.
settings.readers: The closing lines present the poem to its readers (see 10:1-7) as a song for "all the people" to hear.

settings.to: later readers and copyists of the tablet
settings.why: To record the title, the line count of the tablet and of the whole work, the copyist and the date, so the copy could be checked and dated.
settings.readers: The copy was written by Ipiq-Aya, a junior scribe at Sippar, in the twelfth year of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon (his colophon, 12:104-115; SEAL), in the 1600s BC (Millard). Its first readers were scribes in training and the temple and palace circles they served; later copies from Ugarit, Hattusa and Nippur show that the story travelled far in the next centuries.
